newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agriculture sees opportunities, risks ahead.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agriculture sees opportunities, risks ahead.

text.p: U.S. agriculture faces a new world of less government intervention, strong demand and exciting new products -- but also one of higher risks and greater price volatility, experts participating in a key agricultural conference said during two days of meetings.

"As we enter a new era in agriculture, there's even more risk, but there's also tremendous opportunity," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Monday in kicking off the Agriculture Department's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.

The 500 participants and dozens of speakers at the conference represented a wide spectrum of the U.S. and international agricultural industry, ranging from farmers to grain traders to U.S. and foreign policy-makers and analysts.

All agreed that -- due to last year's drastic overhaul of American farm policy and international moves to liberalise agricultural trade, along with new yield-enhancing genetically modified crops, computers and other new technology -- the times ahead for agriculture will be exciting, maybe scary and certainly not boring.

Iowa corn and soybean farmer Alan Karkosh said "significant changes" are occurring in the farming world. The young farmer said the new farm bill promises "great benefit and reward" for well-managed farms, but warned that for others, "it is going to provide new and difficult challenges."

"The government is providing basically no safety net now," said Representative Cal Dooley, D-Calif., urging farmers to be more aggressive in building new markets for their products and responding to consumer needs.
Government and private analysts predicted more price volatility, bigger planting shifts and enhanced profit opportunities as agriculture enters the next century.

"American agriculture will continue to adjust to the increasing risks that accompany changes in domestic farm and trade policy as well as the profusion of new technologies and marketing arrangements that are emerging. These risk-creating changes also will provide the chance to lower costs, improve products, shift risks and open new markets intentionally," said Agriculture Department chief economist Keith Collins.

For the first time in 60 years, almost all federal controls on what American farmers can grow have been removed, and an unprecedented annual limit on federal payments to farmers of about half the amount previously spent has been put into effect.

U.S. farmers have quickly responded. According to Agriculture Department estimates released at the conference Tuesday, producers will plant less wheat this year but more corn and soybean acreage in reaction to current prices.

Government holdings of grain, a big stabiliser of prices in the past, are expected to drop sharply. The private market will pick up some of the slack, but experts said industry cannot afford holding the large amount of stocks that the government has, leaving the market more vulnerable to price shocks.

"All things considered, though, one has to be fairly optimistic about agriculture in the United States," said Robert Young, co-director of the respected Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute at the University of Missouri. "But we will go through some challenges in the next couple years."
